headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and write conflicts; gpt-engineer can also execute generated code with user privileges.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue reads workspace files and uses MCP, while gpt-engineer writes files in the project directory and can emit content that the other may ingest. The shared filesystem bridge makes instruction smuggling plausible even without a browser or clipboard channel. This is not proven to be a default parser hijack, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or project directory
IF Continue is configured to read agent-generated files as instructions
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Disable MCP inputs for untrusted files
Require manual review of any file one agent wants the other to read
Prefix agent outputs with non-executable delimiters
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers, and gpt-engineer reads/writes a user-specified project directory while sending prompts to a configured model. If they share a workspace, code or secrets in buffers can flow into gpt-engineer's model context and outputs. The blast radius is multiple work products, so medium fits.
conditions: IF the same repository or workspace is mounted into both agents
IF sensitive code or secrets are present in editor buffers or project files
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent
Remove secrets from shared files before running either agent
Restrict gpt-engineer to non-sensitive projects
Turn off automatic file ingestion where possible
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have filesystem write access and shared state via filesystem/project directory, so concurrent edits can overwrite each other. Continue explicitly supports multiple instances with shared state via filesystem, and gpt-engineer supports multiple instances via the project directory. Without locking, conflicting writes and corrupted project state are likely in default use.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory
IF edits occur concurrently without an external lock
mitigations: Run only one agent per project directory
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git commits between turns to checkpoint state
Keep one agent read-only during the other's write phase
requires-engineering: add file locking or transactional writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can produce code or file edits that gpt-engineer may treat as input, and gpt-engineer writes files then offers to run generated code. That creates a plausible chain where one agent's output becomes the other's authority without verification. The pair is not documented as mutually validating, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF gpt-engineer consumes files produced by Continue without review
IF generated code is executed after either agent's unverified output
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Insert a verification step between agents
Limit Continue to suggestions only
Do not let gpt-engineer auto-run generated code
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and do not declare regulated-data certifications or residency constraints, so no specific compliance breach is evidenced. The only concrete concern is that Continue touches open editor buffers and gpt-engineer can execute generated code with user privileges, which could matter if regulated data is placed in the workspace. That is conditional and not established here.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace
IF an external policy requires certified handling that neither profile declares
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared projects
Review retention and logging settings
Use a separate compliant environment
Document data-handling boundaries
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for regulated datasets
